newsitem.title: UK: PacifiCorp Energy move keeps bid speculation alive.
newsitem.headline: PacifiCorp Energy move keeps bid speculation alive.

text.p: An agreed 3.7 billion pounds ($6.0 billion) bid for The Energy Group from U.S. based PacifiCorp on Friday kept bid speculation alive in the electricity sector, analysts said, but targets are limited.
"I'm certain there could be more bidders, the problem is that there are few targets left," said one analyst who asked not to be named.

PacifiCorp made the bid at 690 pence per share plus a 5.5 pence dividend after Energy had been forced late on Tuesday to disclose the companies were in talks following of a strong rise in its share price.
But Energy shares closed on Friday down two pence at 646 pence, off a high of 663 pence, pressured by concerns that the new Labour government might hamper the deal.
"There is a good chance the bid might be referred to competition authorities," the analyst said.
That is keeping speculation around other possible bids dampened although regional electricity company (Rec) Southern Electric is still seen as a possible target.

Southern shares, which have risen nearly 40 percent since mid-October as a flurry of bids in the sector left it the only independent regional electricity company (Rec), gained another 3.5 pence on Friday to 436.5 pence.
"Southern is the most obvious target. I think 500 pence per share would be a fair price, possibly more," the analyst said.

Last month, generator PowerGen was rumoured to be interested in buying the last remaining Rec but Southern management has fiercely defended its independence and analysts warned the electricity producer had already been halted on such a move.

Its plans to merge with Rec Midlands Electricity were blocked by the previous Conservative government because it would have created a vertically integrated power group along with a similar deal involving Southern, which was keen at the time to link up with National Power.
Southern was then pipped to the post on a takeover of Southern Water by acquisitive multi-utility Scottish Power, which already owned Rec Manweb.
Midlands Electricity was later sold to U.S. group Avon Energy for 1.73 billion pounds.

Eleven of the original 12 Recs set up at privatisation in 1990 have now been swallowed up, with U.S. companies buying seven as they aim to benefit from the experience of operating under Britain's regulations as the market heads for liberalisation in 1998.
The Energy Group itself controls Rec Eastern Electricity, which was bought in 1995 by Hanson, the once-mighty industrial conglomerate whose demerger gave birth to PacifiCorp's target in February.
But the new Labour government, which won power in a landslide victory on May 1, was fiercely critical of the previous Conservative government's policy both on privatisation and takeovers.
It also has privatised utilities in its sights for a one-off tax on their excess profits, which it will make a central plank of its first budget on July 2.
"You can see the uncertainty over this government's views reflected in share prices," the analyst said.

There is concern that the government might decide to refer the bid for Energy because it controls 10 percent of the country's electricity generation, a problem which a takeover of Southern would not face.

The previous government blocked a planned bid by Southern Co of the U.S. for generator National Power because of its perceived strategic importance, effectively ruling out takeovers for other generators including PowerGen.
Analysts speculated that Scottish Hydro, the generation and supply company which operates in Scotland, could be attractive to predators.
But such a bid would again be likely to face problems over generating assets and the government maintains a controlling "golden share" in the company.
Northern Ireland Electricity was also cited as a possible candidate but also carries a golden share.
Scottish Hydro shares closed down 13 pence at 412 pence while Northern Ireland inched up 1.5 pence to 420 pence.
($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
